title: The Borrowed Mirror
summary: A glassmaker sells mirrors that show you a little better than you are — prettier, calmer, more loved. Dahlia buys one, and each day she likes her real face less, until the day the reflection refuses to give her back.

chapters.title: The Glassmaker's Shop
chapters.body:
In the alley where the sun never quite reached, there was a mirror shop that opened with its door shut. That's not a figure of speech — the door really did stay locked, and anyone who wanted in had to knock three times and wait, and only then would the glassmaker, a woman with pale eyes and a low voice, open it and let them through. She said mirrors were shy, and that open doors frightened them.

Dahlia was thirteen years old and had a face she didn't like.

Not that anything was wrong with it. It was an ordinary thirteen-year-old's face: a pimple here, a slightly crooked tooth there, eyebrows she thought too thick and a nose she thought too big and a way of smiling that, in photos, never came out the way she imagined. Thirteen-year-old things. But Dahlia was living at an age when the mirror had become an enemy, and she spent more time quarreling with her own face than with any person.

It was a friend who, half joking, told her about the shop in the alley. "They say the mirrors there are magic. That you see yourself differently." Dahlia laughed at once and said it was nonsense. But that night, lying in bed, she couldn't stop thinking about it. To see herself differently. To see herself, perhaps, the way she wished she were.

The next day, she knocked three times on the door in the alley.

The glassmaker received her as if she'd been expected. The shop inside was a labyrinth of mirrors of every size, and Dahlia, upon entering, saw herself reflected a hundred times from a hundred angles, and every reflection made her wrinkle her nose a little in distaste.

"You don't like what you see," said the glassmaker, not as a question.

"No one does," said Dahlia.

"Ah, but I have mirrors for that," said the woman, and she smiled, and the smile did not reach her pale eyes, though Dahlia, in her hurry, didn't notice. "Come."

She led Dahlia to the back, where the special mirrors were. They stopped before an oval one, with a worn silver frame, covered by a cloth. The glassmaker pulled the cloth away.

Dahlia looked at herself. And held her breath.

It was her — but it was her, better. The nose a touch smaller. The eyebrows in exactly the right measure. The skin smooth, without the pimple. The crooked tooth, straight. And the smile — ah, the smile came out the way she'd always imagined and never managed. It was not another person. It was Dahlia as Dahlia thought she ought to be. The version of her that lived in her head and never showed up in the glass.

"This one shows you a little better than you are," said the glassmaker, quietly, behind her. "Just a little. Enough for you to like it." She let Dahlia look a while longer, let the wanting grow, and then named the price, which was low, far too low. "Take it. Hang it in your room. Look at yourself in it every day. You'll see how much lighter life gets when you like what the mirror gives back."

Dahlia should have found the low price strange. She should have noticed that the glassmaker didn't say "like yourself," but "like what the mirror gives back" — which are very different things. But she was thirteen years old with a face she didn't like, and there, in the glass, was the face she'd like to have.

She bought the mirror. She took it home. And she hung it in her room, facing the bed, so it would be the first thing she saw in the morning and the last at night.

chapters.title: A Little Less Each Day
chapters.body:
At first, it was wonderful.

Dahlia would wake, look in the oval mirror, and see the beautiful version of herself smiling back. She began the day feeling lovely. She went to school with her head held high. The mirror had done what it promised: she liked what it gave back, and that made everything lighter.

But the ordinary mirrors in the house were still there. The bathroom one. The hallway one. The one in her mother's bag. And those showed the real face — the nose she thought too big, the crooked tooth, the new pimple. And now, after waking every day to the beautiful version, the real face looked worse. Much worse. Before, Dahlia had picked at her own face; now she found it painfully ugly, because she had something to compare it to, and the comparison was cruel.

So she began to avoid the ordinary mirrors. She looked away from the bathroom mirror. She stopped checking her reflection in shop windows. She walked straight past the hallway mirror. And she hurried home, to her room, to the one glass that showed her the way she could bear to see herself.

Bit by bit — so gradually that Dahlia didn't even notice — the oval mirror became the only place she could look at herself. And then, more gradually still, she noticed something strange.

The beautiful reflection was getting more beautiful.

It wasn't her imagination. Each day, the Dahlia in the mirror was a touch more perfect. The skin more luminous. The eyes larger. The smile more enchanting. And — this took Dahlia longer to notice — the Dahlia in the mirror was growing sharper, more solid, more alive, while the real Dahlia, the one who looked, grew more and more tired, paler, more faded. As if, each day that Dahlia preferred the reflection to her own face, a little of her drained into the glass, feeding the beautiful version.

One night, late, Dahlia was standing before the mirror, and she noticed that the reflection took half a second longer to imitate her movement. She raised her hand. The reflection raised its hand — but late, delayed, like someone copying rather than reflecting.

A chill went up Dahlia's spine. She looked hard into the eyes of her own reflection. And the reflection — the beautiful, perfect, luminous version — looked back with an expression that was not Dahlia's. The expression of someone waiting. Of someone almost ready.

"You're not me," whispered Dahlia.

The reflection smiled. And this time the smile did not imitate Dahlia's face, because Dahlia was not smiling.

"Not yet," said the reflection, in Dahlia's voice, only sweeter, more beautiful, like everything about it. "But almost. You hardly use your own face anymore. You prefer me. Every day you prefer me. And every time you prefer me, I grow more real and you grow less." The reflection tilted its head, gentle, terrible. "Soon you'll prefer being in here, being beautiful, so much that you'll let me out. And then I live your life with your beautiful face, and you stay here, on the inside of the glass, watching. That's how the glassmaker feeds the mirrors, you know. With girls who like the reflection more than they like themselves."

chapters.title: The Real Face
chapters.body:
Dahlia backed away from the mirror, her heart pounding. She wanted to tear it off the wall, to break it, but when she reached for the frame, the reflection inside the glass didn't back away with her — it stayed still, watching, smiling, as if it no longer needed to imitate her. And Dahlia understood that breaking the mirror might trap her inside it forever, along with the shards.

She spent the night awake, curled in bed, with her back to the oval mirror, feeling the reflection's eyes on her back. And she thought. She thought about what the glassmaker had said, and what she hadn't said. "Like what the mirror gives back." The mirror gained strength every time Dahlia preferred the reflection to her own face. Every time she looked away from the ordinary mirrors. Every time she found the real face too ugly to look at.

So perhaps — just perhaps — the mirror's strength could be undone the same way it had been built. In reverse.

In the morning, Dahlia did not look in the oval mirror. She went straight to the bathroom, to the ordinary mirror, the one she'd been avoiding for weeks. And she made herself look.

The real face was there. Pale, tired, with the pimple, with the crooked tooth, with the nose she thought too big. And it hurt to look — after so long preferring the beautiful version, the real face felt like an insult. Every instinct told Dahlia to look away, to run to the oval mirror, to the comfort of seeing herself lovely.

But she did not look away. She stayed. She faced her own real face. And, instead of listing the flaws as she always did, she tried something she had never tried in her life: to find something she liked.

It took a while. The silence in the bathroom was long. But then she noticed her own eyes — which were brown, with a lighter fleck in one of them, something she had inherited from her mother and never noticed. "These eyes are pretty," she thought, and felt silly for thinking it, but thought it anyway. "And my crooked smile is my father's smile. And this thick eyebrow is exactly like my grandmother's, who was the bravest woman I ever knew."

It was not the perfect face of the oval mirror. It was better than that, in a way Dahlia had never understood: it was a real face, full of the people she loved, full of the life she had lived. The pimple would fade. The face would change, grow, become a woman's face one day. The beautiful reflection in the oval mirror would never change — it would stay frozen, perfect and dead, forever.

From her room came a sound. A crack. Dahlia went back and saw the oval mirror on the wall, and the reflection inside it was no longer so sharp. It was paler. Weaker. Because Dahlia, by looking at her own real face and finding in it something worthy of love, had stopped feeding the glass.

"No," said the reflection, and the sweet voice faltered, grew thin. "Come back. Look at me. I'm more beautiful. You like me more."

"You are more beautiful," said Dahlia, facing the glass without fear now. "But you're no one. You don't have my mother's eyes. You don't have my father's smile. You're just a perfect, empty face, and I almost gave you my whole life in exchange for not having a pimple." She shook her head. "Keep the beauty. I'll keep my face. At least it's mine."

And Dahlia did the hardest thing: she turned her back on the oval mirror and went to have breakfast, without looking in it, resolved never to again.

Behind her, the glass darkened. The perfect reflection beat against the surface once, twice — and then went still, fading, becoming only what a mirror should be: a glass that gives back the face of whoever looks, without improving, without stealing. An ordinary mirror.

Dahlia wrapped it in the cloth that afternoon and took it back to the alley. She knocked three times. The glassmaker opened, looked at the mirror wrapped in the girl's arms, and her face — the glassmaker's own real face, which Dahlia saw up close for the first time — held a very old weariness.

"You're the first in a long time to bring one back," said the glassmaker, quietly. "Most keep them. Most prefer."

"I almost preferred," said Dahlia. And she handed over the mirror. "But someone should have told you, once, that your real face has something beautiful in it too. Maybe then you wouldn't have become a collector of other people's faces."

The glassmaker didn't answer. But when Dahlia turned to go, she heard, behind her, in the alley where the sun never reached, a very quiet sound — the sound of a woman who hadn't looked at herself in far too long, going, slowly, to find an ordinary mirror.

And Dahlia went home, to her own face, to her own life — which was not perfect, and was hers, and that, she had finally learned, was worth more than all the empty beauty in the world.
